reader.summary: South Korea's economy delivered a spectacular week as October exports nearly doubled year-on-year, driven by an AI-fueled semiconductor boom that pushed third-quarter GDP growth above forecasts and brought the country closer to its one-trillion-dollar annual export target. On the security front, tensions with North Korea escalated sharply: Pyongyang fired around ten ballistic missiles toward the East Sea, positioned howitzer batteries near the border, denounced South Korean-US air-defense drills, and told the United Nations it had fabricated a landmine incident, while Seoul vowed a firm response and considered deploying assets toward the Strait of Hormuz. In domestic politics, prosecutors in the former President Yoon martial-law case pressed for the death penalty, a striking escalation in the post-coup reckoning. A fire engulfed Seoul's last remaining shantytown, forcing hundreds to evacuate before crews extinguished the blaze. Regulators fined Google and Apple over app-store payment practices, and three financial firms including crypto exchange Bithumb reported data breaches. The US, South Korea, and Japan jointly called for North Korea's complete denuclearisation, but Seoul worried about being sidelined as Washington reached out to Pyongyang.

display.eli5:
South Korea is dealing with a lot at once. North Korea just fired about ten missiles and parked heavy guns near the border, and Seoul promised to hit back hard. Meanwhile, the country's chip factories are printing money because of the AI boom, and a former president is facing a possible death sentence for his martial-law blunder.

North Korea keeps testing the border to show it still has teeth, and Seoul wants to prove it won't be pushed around. The chip boom is happening because data centers around the world need more and more AI processors, and South Korean factories make some of the best ones. The Yoon case is about accountability after he tried to seize power with the military.

Next week, Seoul will announce a concrete military response to the missiles, and a big chip company will probably announce a new factory or order that keeps the export boom going. The court will also make a ruling on whether to accept the death-penalty request and set a trial date.

The surprise that would make people sit up is if South Korea actually sends ships or planes to the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East. That would be a big step for a country that usually stays close to home, and it would signal that Seoul is ready to play a bigger role in global security.

US and South Korean officials assessed little chance of a Trump-Kim meeting this year.
